title: PostgreSQL: the default database, and how far it stretches
dek: PostgreSQL is where most designs should start: transactions, SQL, rich indexes, JSON, geospatial queries and a huge set of extensions. Here is what is going on underneath (row versions, processes, the write-ahead log), how it scales, and where it stops.

items: PostgreSQL keeps old and new versions of rows side by side (MVCC), so readers never block writers. VACUUM cleans up the old versions.
Each connection is a separate server process, so many app servers need a pooler such as PgBouncer in front.
One primary with replicas goes a long way: thousands of writes and tens of thousands of reads a second on good hardware. Beyond that, partition, then shard (for example with Citus).

body.cap: Readers see a snapshot, so a long report and a stream of price changes don't wait for each other. The price is old versions that someone has to clean up.

items: Every transaction reads a consistent snapshot. Read committed (the default) takes a new snapshot per statement; repeatable read keeps one for the whole transaction; serializable also detects conflicts and aborts one transaction to retry.
Writers still lock the rows they change, so two updates of the same row wait for each other.
Autovacuum removes dead versions in the background. Tables with heavy updates may need it tuned to run more often.
A transaction left open for hours stops cleanup everywhere and lets tables bloat. Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`.

body.cap: PostgreSQL wants a few dozen busy connections, not thousands of idle ones. A pooler is the usual answer once there are many app servers.

items: Size the pool by cores and disks, not by app servers: often a few times the CPU count of the database machine.
Transaction pooling suits short web requests; session pooling keeps per-session features working.
Managed services offer their own proxies that pool connections and smooth failovers.

items: `jsonb` stores flexible attributes with indexes, covering many uses of a document store.
Extensions add whole capabilities: PostGIS for maps, pg_stat_statements for finding slow queries, pgvector for similarity search.
Declarative partitioning splits a big table by range or list (orders by month), so old months can be dropped in a second.
Streaming replication ships the write-ahead log to replicas, asynchronously by default or synchronously for chosen standbys.
Logical replication sends row changes, which can feed another database version, a subset of tables or a change-data-capture pipeline.
Failover isn't built in: use a managed service, or a tool such as Patroni with a consensus store to promote a standby and stop the old primary.
Vertical first: large machines with fast disks handle most products for a long time.
Read replicas and caches for reads; partitioning for very large tables; archiving for old rows.
Sharding when one primary can't take the writes: Citus distributes tables across nodes, or the application routes by key.
The usual sharp edges: long transactions, missing indexes, too many connections, and schema changes that rewrite or lock a big table.
Start with PostgreSQL unless a requirement rules it out, and say which requirement would.
Sketch tables, keys and the indexes for the main queries.
Mention a pooler, replicas for reads, a synchronous standby for failover, and backups with point-in-time recovery.
Know the next step at scale: partitioning, then sharding by a key.

body.x: Row versions are stamped with 32-bit transaction IDs, which wrap around after about 2 billion (200 crore). VACUUM 'freezes' old rows so the wrap is harmless. If vacuuming is blocked for a very long time on a busy database, PostgreSQL eventually stops accepting writes to protect the data. Monitoring how old the oldest unfrozen transaction is, and never blocking autovacuum for days, prevents it.
